note: Launch registry (§5.1). This file is the seed for the `platforms` table; served to clients at runtime from the server/edge cache — never hardcoded into client bundles. Selector fields are placeholders until extension work (Phase 5) verifies them against live DOMs. All capability data is perishable: re-verify via the PKB ingestion pipeline (§6.3). | v1.1.0 (2026-07-12): added doc-curated `modes` per platform (V1.2) — perishable, refresh from official docs.

quirks: Negative prompts are unreliable for image generation — phrase exclusions positively (describe what SHOULD be present)
Responds well to conversational, full-sentence phrasing rather than keyword lists
Aspect-ratio requests mentioned only in passing are often ignored — state them as an explicit constraint
syntax_rules: Plain natural language; no special parameter flags in the consumer web app
For image tasks, lead with subject and action, then style and mood in the same sentence or a short follow-on sentence

modes.name: Gemini 2.5 Flash
modes.notes: The default fast model — lowest latency and cost. Great for everyday chat, summaries, and extraction; hand harder reasoning to Pro or Thinking.

modes.name: Gemini 2.5 Pro
avoid_for: trivial lookups where Flash is cheaper
modes.notes: The high-capability model with a very large context window — pick it for long inputs, serious code work, and analysis.

modes.name: Thinking (extended reasoning)
modes.notes: Spends visible reasoning tokens before answering — slower and pricier, but materially better on multi-step problems.

modes.name: Image generation (Imagen)
modes.notes: Gemini's image mode. Describe the SHOULD-be-present content positively; negative prompts are unreliable here.

modes.name: Deep Research
modes.notes: Agentic multi-source research producing a cited report — use for breadth, not speed.

quirks: Strong system/persona adherence when the role is stated up front in the first message
Verbose by default — explicit length constraints materially change output
Image generation via integrated tooling responds to full descriptive sentences, not tag lists
syntax_rules: Markdown structure (headings, numbered steps) improves multi-part instruction following
State role/persona first, task second, constraints third, output format last

modes.name: GPT-4o
avoid_for: hardest math/logic where a reasoning model wins
modes.notes: The general-purpose multimodal default — balanced quality, speed, and cost.

modes.name: o3 (reasoning)
modes.notes: Deliberate reasoning model — slower, but strongest on multi-step problems and hard code.

modes.name: o4-mini
modes.notes: Small fast reasoning model — most of o3's skill at a fraction of the latency/cost.

modes.name: Image generation
modes.notes: ChatGPT's image mode. Handles long natural-language scene descriptions and in-image text well.

quirks: Documented to respond well to XML-style tags for separating instruction sections (<instructions>, <example>, <data>)
Benefits measurably from explicit step-by-step reasoning requests on complex tasks
Follows positive instructions more reliably than negations
syntax_rules: Use tagged sections for multi-part prompts
Put long reference/context material before the question or instruction
Request output format explicitly, ideally with a short example

modes.name: Claude Sonnet
modes.notes: The everyday balanced model — strong writing and code at moderate cost.

modes.name: Claude Haiku
modes.notes: The fastest and most cost-efficient Claude model — ideal for high-volume production workloads, classification, and extraction tasks.

modes.name: Claude Opus
modes.notes: The frontier model — pick it when quality matters more than cost.

modes.name: Extended thinking
modes.notes: Lets Claude reason step-by-step before answering — enable for problems with a right answer.

quirks: Comma-separated dense descriptor phrases outperform full sentences
Word order matters: earlier tokens carry more weight
Supports explicit parameter flags (--ar, --v, --style, --no) appended at the end
The --no parameter is the supported negative-prompt mechanism; in-text negation ('without X') is unreliable
syntax_rules: Structure: subject descriptors, scene/setting, style/medium, lighting, composition, then parameter flags
Parameters go last: e.g. `--ar 16:9 --style raw`
Avoid filler words ('a picture of', 'please')

modes.name: Version 7 (default)
modes.notes: The default engine — best coherence and photorealism.

modes.name: Niji (anime)
modes.notes: Anime/illustration-tuned engine — dramatically better for manga and character art styles.

modes.name: Raw style
avoid_for: when you want Midjourney's opinionated aesthetic
modes.notes: Reduces the house beautification so your prompt is followed more literally.

quirks: Dedicated negative-prompt field — exclusions belong there, not in the main prompt
Supports attention weighting syntax in most UIs: (word:1.3)
Tag-style comma-separated descriptors outperform prose; quality tags (e.g. 'highly detailed', 'sharp focus') have documented effect
syntax_rules: Main prompt: comma-separated descriptors ordered subject → style → quality tags
Negative prompt: comma-separated exclusion list (e.g. 'blurry, extra limbs, watermark, text')
Keep individual descriptor phrases short; prefer many precise tags over one long sentence

modes.name: SD 3.5 Large
modes.notes: Highest-quality tier — best prompt adherence and detail; slower per image.

modes.name: SD 3.5 Large Turbo
modes.notes: Distilled fast tier — iterate compositions cheaply, then rerun winners on Large.

quirks: Agentic CLI coding tool — reads/edits files and runs commands, not a chat box; prompts are task instructions in a terminal
Slash commands (e.g. /init, /clear, /compact, custom skills) change behavior; plan mode separates planning from editing
Responds best to a clear objective plus constraints; it will explore the codebase itself rather than needing files pasted in
CLAUDE.md files in the repo are auto-loaded as persistent instructions
syntax_rules: State the goal, the acceptance criteria, and any files/dirs to focus on or avoid
Prefer 'do X and verify with the test suite' over pasting large code blocks
Reference existing conventions instead of re-specifying them; the tool reads the repo

modes.name: Interactive CLI
modes.notes: Repo-aware agentic coding in the terminal — give it goals and constraints, not keystrokes.

quirks: IDE with inline edit (Cmd/Ctrl+K), chat, and an agent mode; @-symbols pull files/docs/symbols into context
.cursorrules / project rules files set persistent coding conventions
Inline edits work best scoped to a selection; broad refactors belong in agent/composer mode
Explicitly @-referencing the right files beats hoping it infers context
syntax_rules: Use @file / @folder / @docs to ground the request in specific context
Keep inline-edit instructions to a single, local change
Encode house style in a rules file rather than repeating it each prompt

modes.name: Agent mode
modes.notes: Plans and executes multi-file changes autonomously — the mode for real feature work.

modes.name: Ask mode
modes.notes: Read-only Q&A over your codebase — explanations without touching files.

quirks: Completion + chat; chat supports slash commands (/explain, /fix, /tests, /doc) and #-file / @-participant references
Leading comments and clear function/variable names strongly steer completions
Open relevant files in the editor — Copilot uses neighboring tabs as context
For chat, name the file/symbol explicitly rather than relying on cursor position
syntax_rules: Write a descriptive comment or signature before expecting a good completion
Use chat slash commands for structured tasks (/tests, /fix)
Reference files with # in chat to ground answers

modes.name: Inline completions
modes.notes: As-you-type suggestions — steer with nearby comments and good function names.

modes.name: Copilot Chat
modes.notes: Conversational panel with slash-commands (/tests, /fix) and workspace context.

quirks: Answer engine that searches the live web and cites sources — treat it like a research query, not a creative prompt
Focus modes (Web, Academic, etc.) and source constraints change results; specifying recency/domain helps
Concise, keyword-rich questions retrieve better than long narrative prompts
Ask for citations/comparisons explicitly to get structured, sourced answers
syntax_rules: Phrase as a specific researchable question
State time range, domains, or source type when it matters (e.g. 'peer-reviewed, last 2 years')
Ask for a sourced comparison/table when you want structure

modes.name: Quick search
modes.notes: Fast web-grounded answers with citations — the default for lookups.

modes.name: Deep Research
modes.notes: Runs many searches and synthesizes a cited report — minutes, not seconds.

quirks: Follows explicit, numbered instructions reliably; benefits from clear delimiters between context and task
Strong at structured JSON output when the schema is stated explicitly
syntax_rules: Plain natural language; separate distinct sections (context, task, format) with clear headers or line breaks
State the desired output format explicitly, especially for JSON or tables

quirks: Runs a rotating set of open-weight models; keep prompts model-agnostic and explicit rather than relying on a specific model's habits
Open models follow few-shot examples well — include one or two when format matters
syntax_rules: Plain natural language; lead with a clear instruction, then context, then any examples
For structured output, show a concrete example of the exact format wanted

quirks: Conversational and willing to reason step by step when asked; benefits from an explicit request to think before answering
Can access real-time context on X — state when you want current information versus general knowledge
syntax_rules: Plain natural language; ask for step-by-step reasoning explicitly when the task is analytical
Be explicit about tone — Grok defaults to a casual, witty register

quirks: The reasoning (R1) mode exposes chain-of-thought — do NOT add your own 'think step by step' instruction, it already reasons and extra instructions can degrade output
For the reasoning model, keep the prompt to a clear problem statement and let it reason
syntax_rules: Plain natural language; state the problem and desired final-answer format, not the reasoning process
Strong at code and math — provide exact constraints and edge cases
